'''betrayer''' (bẹ̄-trā′ėr), ''n.'' One who betrays; a traitor; a seducer.

'''betrayment†''' (bẹ̄-trā′mẹnt), ''n.'' [< ''betray'' + ''-ment.''] Betrayal; the state of being betrayed.
{{smaller block|Confessing him to be innocent whose ''betrayment'' they had sought.
{{right|''Udall'', Com. on Mat. xxvii.}}}}

'''betrend†''' (bẹ̄-trend′), ''v. t.'' [ME. ''betrenden''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''trend.''] To wind about; twist; turn round.
{{smaller block|<poem>Aboute a tre with many a twiste
''Bytrent'' and wrythe the soote wodebynde.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 1231.}}}}

'''betrim''' (bẹ̄-trim′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''betrimmed'', ppr. ''betrimming''. [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''trim.''] To trim; set in order; decorate; beautify.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy banks with pioned and twilled brims,
Which spongy April at thy hest ''betrims''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1.}}}}

'''betroth''' (bẹ̄-trôth′ or -trōth′), ''v. t.'' [Early mod. E. also ''betrothe, betroath, betrouth'', < ME. ''betrouthen, betreuthen, bitreuthien'', betroth, < ''bi-'', ''be-'', + ''treuthe, treowthe'', < AS. ''treówth'', troth, truth: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''troth, truth.''] '''1.''' To contract to give in marriage to another; promise or pledge one’s troth for the marriage of; affiance.
{{smaller block|<poem>You, to remove that siege of grief from her,
''Betroth’d'' and would have married her perforce
To County Paris.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., v. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' To engage to take in marriage; pledge one’s troth to marry.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|betrash|537|betterment}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''betrash†''', ''v. t.'' See ''betraise''.

'''betray''' (bē-trā′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''betrayen'', ''betrain'', < ''be-'' + ''traien'', betray, < OF. ''traïr'', F. ''trahir'', < L. ''tradere'', deliver, give over: see ''traitor'', ''treason'', ''tradition''. The form of ''betray'' was influenced by that of ''bewray'', a quite different word.]   '''1.''' To deliver to, or expose to the power of, an enemy by treachery or disloyalty: as, an officer ''betrayed'' the city.
{{smaller block|The Son of man shall be ''betrayed'' into the hands of men.
{{right|Mat. xvii. 22.}}}}
'''2.''' To violate by fraud or unfaithfulness; be unfaithful in keeping or upholding: as, to ''betray'' a trust.
{{smaller block|''Betray’d'' her cause and mine. {{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, v.}}}}
'''3.''' To act treacherously to; be disloyal to; disappoint the hopes or expectations of.
{{smaller block|Do not ''betray'' me, sir. I fear you love Mistress Page.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I will ''betray''
Tawny-finn’d fishes; my bended hook shall pierce
Their slimy jaws.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|But when I rise, I shall find my legs ''betraying'' me.
{{right|''Boswell.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Men of unquiet minds and violent ambition followed a fearfully eccentric course, . . . served and ''betrayed'' all parties in turn. {{right|''Macaulay'', Sir William Temple.}}}}
'''4.''' To deceive; beguile; mislead; seduce.
{{smaller block|<poem>Far, far beneath the shallow maid
He left believing and ''betrayed.''</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', The Giaour.}}}}
{{smaller block|Our impatience ''betrays'' us into rash and foolish alliances which no God attends.
{{right|''Emerson'', Essays, 1st ser., p. 195.}}}}

'''5.''' To reveal or disclose in violation of confidence; make known through breach of faith or obligation: as, to ''betray'' a person’s secrets or designs.
{{smaller block|Secrets are rarely ''betrayed'' or discovered according to any programme our fear has sketched out.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, v. 5.}}}}

'''6.''' To show in true character; allow to be seen; permit to appear in spite of will or desire.
{{smaller block|Be swift to hear, but cautious of your tongue, lest you ''betray'' your ignorance.
{{right|''Watts.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And scarcely look or tone ''betrays''
How the heart strives beneath its chain.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Mogg Megone, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>My own too-fearful guilt,
Simpler than any child, ''betrays'' itself.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Guinevere.}}}}

'''7.''' To indicate; give indication or evidence of: said of something not obvious at first view, or that would otherwise be concealed.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yon azure smoke ''betrays'' the lurking town.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Prelude, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|All the names in the country ''betray'' great antiquity.
{{right|''Bryant.''}}}}
{{smaller block|A turned leaf, a broken twig, the faintest film of smoke against the sky, ''betrayed'' to him the passage or presence of an enemy.
{{right|''J. F. Clarke'', Self-Culture, v.}}}}

'''betrayal''' (bē-trā′al), ''n.''   [< ''betray'' + ''-al.'']   The act of betraying.
{{smaller block|Gained his freedom by the ''betrayal'' of his country’s cause.
{{right|''S. Sharpe'', Hist. of Egypt, xii.}}}}
{{smaller block|He seldom lost his self-control, and shrank with the most sensitive pride from any noticeable ''betrayal'' of emotion.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, vi. 7.}}}}

'''betrayer''' (bẹ̄-trā′ėr), ''n.'' One who betrays; a traitor; a seducer.

'''betrayment†''' (bẹ̄-trā′mẹnt), ''n.''   [< ''betray'' + ''-ment.'']   Betrayal; the state of being betrayed.
{{smaller block|Confessing him to be innocent whose ''betrayment'' they had sought.
{{right|''Udall'', Com. on Mat. xxvii.}}}}

'''betrend†''' (bẹ̄-trend′), ''v. t.''   [ME. ''betrenden''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''trend.'']   To wind about; twist; turn round.
{{smaller block|<poem>Aboute a tre with many a twiste
''Bytrent'' and wrythe the soote wodebynde.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 1231.}}}}

'''betrim''' (bẹ̄-trim′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''betrimmed'', ppr. ''betrimming''.   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''trim.'']   To trim; set in order; decorate; beautify.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy banks with pioned and twilled brims,
Which spongy April at thy hest ''betrims''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1.}}}}

'''betroth''' (bẹ̄-trôth′ or -trōth′), ''v. t.''   [Early mod. E. also ''betrothe, betroath, betrouth'', < ME. ''betrouthen, betreuthen, bitreuthien'', betroth, < ''bi-'', ''be-'', + ''treuthe, treowthe'', < AS. ''treówth'', troth, truth: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''troth, truth.'']   '''1.''' To contract to give in marriage to another; promise or pledge one’s troth for the marriage of; affiance.
{{smaller block|<poem>You, to remove that siege of grief from her,
''Betroth’d'' and would have married her perforce
To County Paris.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., v. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' To engage to take in marriage; pledge one’s troth to marry.

{{smaller block|What man is there that hath ''betrothed'' a wife and hath not taken her?
{{right|Deut. xx. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To her, my lord,
Was I ''betroth’d'' ere I saw Hermia.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iv. 1.}}}}
'''3†.''' To nominate to a bishopric in order to consecration.
{{smaller block|If any person be consecrated a bishop to that church whereunto he was not before ''betrothed.''
{{right|''Ayliffe'', Parergon.}}}}

'''betrothal''' (bẹ̄-trôth′- or bẹ̄-trōth′al), ''n.''   [< ''betroth'' + ''-al.'']   The act of betrothing; betrothment.
{{smaller block|The feast of ''betrothal.''
{{right|''Longfellow'', Evangeline, iv.}}}}

'''betrothment''' (bẹ̄-trôth′- or bẹ̄-trōth′mẹnt), ''n.''   [< ''betroth'' + ''-ment.'']   A mutual and formal promise or contract made for or by a man and a woman with a view to their marriage; betrothal; the act or state of being betrothed, or promised in marriage.
{{smaller block|How the strange ''betrothment'' was to end.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess.}}}}

'''betrust''' (bẹ̄-trust′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''trust.'']   '''1.''' To intrust; commit to another in confidence of fidelity.
{{smaller block|Whatsoever you would ''betrust'' to your memory, let it be disposed in a proper method.
{{right|''Watts.''}}}}
'''2.''' To confide in.
{{smaller block|To esteem themselves Maisters, both of that great trust which they serve, and of the People that ''betrusted'' them.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xiii.}}}}
[Rare in both senses.]

'''betrustment''' (bẹ̄-trust′mẹnt), ''n.''   [< ''betrust'' + ''-ment.'']   The act of intrusting; the thing intrusted. [Rare.]

'''betso†, betsa†''' (bet′sō, -sä̤), ''n.''   [< It. ''bezzo'' (pron. bet′so), farthing, piece of money; appar. same as It. ''pezzo'', a piece, bit (see ''piece''); but cf. G. ''betz'', ''bätz'', also ''batzen'', a small Swiss coin: see ''batz''.]   A small copper coin of Venice, current in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. {{smaller|In the system established in 1750 it was equal to a quarter of a United States cent, being the fortieth part of a lira piccola; a bagattino.}}
{{smaller block|The last and least [coin] is the ''betsa'', which is half a sol; that is, almost a farthing.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities (ed. 1776), II. 69.}}}}

'''bett†, bette†''', ''adv.'' Middle English forms of ''bet''<sup>1</sup>.

'''better'''<sup>1</sup> (bet′ėr), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ME. ''bettere'', ''betere'', < AS. ''betera'', ''betra'' = OFries. ''betere'', ''betre'' = OS. ''betara'', ''betera'' = D. ''beter'' = OHG. ''bezziro'', MHG. ''bezzer'', G. ''besser'' = Icel. ''betri'' = Sw. ''bättre'' = Dan. ''bedre'' = Goth. ''batiza''; compar. with weak inflection; with superl. ''best'', < ME. ''beste'', < AS. ''betst'', ''betest'' = OFries. ''beste'' = OS. ''betsto'' = D. ''best'' = OHG. ''bezzisto'', MHG. ''bezzist'', ''best'', G. ''best'' = Icel. ''beztr'', older ''baztr'', = Sw. ''bäst'' = Dan. ''bedst'' = Goth. ''batists''; with regular compar. and superl. suffixes from a positive not in use, Teut. *''bat'', of which the compar., with loss of the suffix, appears in the AS., ME., and early mod. E. adv. ''bet'': see ''bet''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' As comparative of ''good'': (''a'') Of superior quality or excellence, whether personal, physical, mental, moral, or social, essential or acquired: as, he is a ''better'' man than his brother; ''better'' times are at hand; a ''better'' position.
{{smaller block|Man’s ''better'' nature triumphed then.
{{right|''Bryant'', The Prairies.}}}}
{{smaller block|Our institutions had been so good that they had educated us into a capacity for ''better'' institutions.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Mirabeau.}}}}
(''b'') Of superior value, use, fitness, acceptableness, etc.; more profitable or suitable for a purpose; more useful, eligible, or desirable: as, copper is a ''better'' conductor than iron.
{{smaller block|''Better'' is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith. {{right|Prov. xv. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Sleep
Doth, in my estimate of good, appear
A ''better'' state than waking; death than sleep.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion, iii.}}}}
(''c'') Larger; greater: as, the ''better'' part of a day was spent in shopping.
{{smaller block|<poem>You are as a candle, the ''better'' part burnt out.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>How have we wander’d, that the ''better'' part
Of this good night is perish’d!</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, ii. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' As comparative of ''well'': (''a'') More in accordance with one’s wish or desire; more satisfactory. (''b'') More healthy; having sounder health. (''c'') More just, right, or proper.—'''Better arm.''' {{smaller|See ''arm''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''Better half,''' {{smaller|a wife. [Colloq.]}}—'''To be better.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To be improved, as in health, estate, etc.: as, the patient ''is better''. (''b'') To be quite well again; be fully recovered. [Scotland.]}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' That which has superior excellence; that which is better.
{{smaller block|That ideal ''better'', towards which both men and institutions must progress, if they would not retrograde.
{{right|''Huxley'', Universities.}}}}

'''2.''' A superior; one who has a claim to precedence on account of rank, age, merit, skill, power, or office: as, give place to your ''betters.'' [In this sense generally used in the plural, and with a possessive pronoun.]
{{smaller block|In al Yngleloud was non hys ''beter.''
{{right|''Rich. C. de L.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Their ''betters'' would hardly be found. {{right|''Hooker.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Thou poor shadow of a soldier, I will make thee know my master keeps servants thy ''betters'' in quality and performance. {{right|''Ford'', ’Tis Pity, i. 2.}}}}

{{smaller|'''The better.''' (''a'') Improvement: generally in the adverbial phrase ''for the better'', that is, in the direction of improvement.}}
{{smaller block|If I have altered him anywhere ''for the better.''
{{right|''Dryden'', Preface to Fables.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Advantage; superiority; victory: chiefly in the phrases ''to get, gain'', or ''have the better of'' (a person or thing).}}
{{smaller block|Dionysius, his countryman, in an epistle to Pompey, after an express comparison, affords him ''the better of'' Thucydides. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err.}}}}
{{smaller block|She took her leave, charmed with the prospect of finally ''getting the better of'' the only woman in London whom she acknowledged as her equal in subtlety and intrigue.
{{right|''J. Hawthorne'', Dust, p. 334.}}}}

'''better<sup>1</sup>''' (bet′ėr), ''adv.'' (comparative of ''well, adv.'').   [< ME. ''better, beter, betre'', < AS. ''betere, betre''; with superl. ''best'', < ME. ''best'', < AS. ''betst, betōst''; prop. neut. acc. of the adj.: see ''better''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'' The older adv. was ''bet'': see ''bet''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' In a more excellent way or manner: as, to behave ''better''; the land is ''better'' cultivated and the government ''better'' administered.
{{smaller block|The plays of Shakspeare were ''better'' acted, ''better'' edited, and ''better'' known than they had ever been.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Moore’s Byron.}}}}
'''2.''' In a superior degree: as, to know a man ''better'' than some one else knows him.
{{smaller block|Which is the ''better'' able to defend himself: a strong man with nothing but his fists, or a paralytic cripple encumbered with a sword which he cannot lift?
{{right|''Macaulay'', Utilitarian Theory of Government.}}}}
'''3.''' More, without any idea of superior excellence: as, it is ''better'' than a mile to the town. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Dorlcote Mill has been in our family a hundred year and ''better''.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To be better off''', to be in improved circumstances.}}
{{smaller block|The mechanic teaches us how we may in a small degree ''be better off'' than we were. The Utilitarian advises us with great pomp to be as well off as we can.
{{right|''Macaulay'', West. Reviewer’s Def. of Mill.}}}}
{{smaller block|Men had become Romans; they were proud of the Roman name; . . . they felt that they ''were better off'' as members of a civilized community ordered by law than they could be under the dominion of any barbarian.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 126.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To go one better.''' See ''go, v. t.''}}

'''better'''<sup>1</sup> (bet′ėr), ''v.''   [< ME. ''bettren'', ''betren'', < AS. ''beterian'', ''betrian'', intr., be better, ''ge-beterian'', ''ge-betrian'', trans., make better (= OFries. ''beteria'' = Icel. ''betra'' = Sw. ''bättra'' = Dan. ''bedre'' = OHG. ''bezzirōn'', MHG. G. ''bessern''; cf. OS. ''betian'', < ''bet'', the older compar. adv.), < ''betera'', better: see ''better''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make better; improve; ameliorate; increase the good qualities of: as, manure ''betters'' land; discipline may ''better'' the morals.
{{smaller block|The cause of his taking upon him our nature was to ''better'' the quality, and to advance the condition thereof.
{{right|''Hooker.''}}}}
'''2.''' To improve upon; surpass; exceed; outdo.
{{smaller block|He hath borne himself beyond the promise of his age; . . . he hath, indeed, better ''bettered'' expectation than you must expect of me to tell you how. {{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>What you do
Still ''betters'' what is done. ''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 3.</poem>}}
'''3.''' To advance the interest of; support; give advantage to.
{{smaller block|<poem>Weapons more violent, when next we meet,
May serve to ''better'' us and worse our foes.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 440.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' ''Amend, Improve, Better'', etc. (see ''amend''), meliorate, promote.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To grow better; become better; improve: as, his condition is ''bettering''. [Rare.]

'''better<sup>2</sup>''' (bet′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''bet''<sup>2</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who lays bets or wagers. Also ''bettor''.
{{smaller block|Be able to give them the character of every bowler or ''better'' on the green. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, i. 1.}}}}

'''bettering-house†''' (bet′ėr-ing-hous″), ''n.'' A reformatory.
{{smaller block|Soldiers buried in this ground, from the hospital and the ''bettering-house.'' {{right|''Annals of Phil. and Penn.'', I. 406.}}}}

'''betterment''' (bet′ėr-mẹnt), ''n.''   [< ''better''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', + ''-ment.'']   '''1.''' A making better; improvement.—'''2.''' In ''American law'', an improvement of real property which adds to its value otherwise than by mere repairs: generally used in the plural.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
